newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian debt futures surge on weak retail data.
newsitem.headline: Australian debt futures surge on weak retail data.

text.p: *Australian debt futures surged after retail trade fell for the second consecutive month in April, fuelling speculation that the Reserve Bank will ease policy again.
*September bills touch 94.63, equating to 5.37 percent cash.

Australian debt futures surged after retail trade fell for the second consecutive month in April, fuelling speculation that last Friday's official rate cut to 5.5 percent may not be the last this cycle.
Retail trade dropped 1.7 percent, when a 0.5 percent rise had been forecast, and after a 0.3 percent fall in March, the series' first double negative reading since July/August 1993.

September bill futures jumped to a contract high of 94.63, equating to a cash rate of 5.37 percent, while December bills were close to wiping out any thoughts of a tightening by the end of the year, rallying to 94.46.

"The data certainly adds to the speculation of another rate cut, because it's a case of that if the consumer doesn't come in, employment will never kick-in," said Annette Beacher, senior economist at Citibank Australia.
"We're still less than a 50 percent chance of rate cut, but that's not going to stop the market's running ahead," she added.

By the end of the morning session at 12.30 p.m. (0130 GMT), the June three-year bond contract was testing 93.80, the highest level for a front position since December 1996, and where a break would take the market to levels not seen February 1994.

The market had already been hyped up about a further rate cut in after hours trading following comments by Prime Minister John Howard, saying that while Australia had seen significant interest rate cuts, real interest rates remain high.
The long end also rallied on the data and saw the 10-year spread to the U.S. compress to its lowest level in three years.

"In the short term those low margins will hold. But there are a few risks down the track if rate cut expectations drop out, and then if we see a bit of damage on the U.S. bond market if there are rate rises there," said Nigel Stapledon, chief economist at Westpac Banking Corp.
